title: Echo Canyon Hike
sum: On a hike through Echo Canyon, cousins Lucia and Mateo chase echoes from wall to wall and time each one, until Mateo's whole message finally comes back at Echo Point.

cast.d: Mateo's cousin, nine, who times everything and writes it in her spiral notebook
cast.look: a nine-year-old girl with a long dark braid, a green sun hat, a yellow backpack and a small spiral notebook

cast.d: Lucia's cousin, eight, loud and funny and always ready to shout
cast.look: an eight-year-old boy with short black hair, a red cap worn backward, an orange T-shirt and dusty sneakers

cast.d: Mateo's mom, who has hiked Echo Canyon ten times and wears a big sports watch
cast.look: a woman in her thirties with curly dark hair tied up, sunglasses, a blue hiking shirt and a big black sports watch

cast.d: the park ranger who counts the bats that sleep under Bat Ledge
cast.look: a woman with short black hair, a tan ranger uniform, a wide flat-brimmed hat and a clipboard

p: The wooden sign at the trailhead said ECHO CANYON TRAIL, and under that, ECHO POINT 4 KM. Lucia copied every word into her spiral notebook, even the little arrow. Her cousin Mateo did not copy anything, because he was too busy cupping his hands around his mouth.
“HELLO!” he yelled across the parking lot, as loud as he could. The only answer came from a man loading a cooler into his truck. He looked up, waved, and called back, “Hello to you too, buddy.”
Mateo's arms dropped to his sides. “This whole canyon is broken.” His mom, Aunt Rosa, just pulled her backpack straps tight. She had hiked this trail ten times. “Wait for the walls,” she said.

The trail dipped into a dry, sandy wash and wound between big boulders. Soon the canyon walls began to rise on both sides, red and orange, with stripes like a layer cake. By the first bend, they stood taller than ten houses stacked up. Lucia tipped her head back so far that her sun hat fell off.
Far across the wash, one wall faced them like a giant flat door. Lucia picked up her hat, shook out the sand, and clapped once, hard. A moment later, a smaller clap came back from the rock.

Mateo spun around with his mouth wide open. Then he sucked in a huge breath and shouted his favorite word, “PIZZA!” For a second, nothing happened. Then the canyon answered in a smaller voice, “pizza.” Mateo fell over in the sand, laughing so hard that his cap rolled away.

“It works,” he said when he could talk again. “The canyon likes pizza.” Aunt Rosa laughed and shook her head. “The canyon likes hard rock,” she said. “Your voice hits that wall and bounces back, like a tennis ball off a garage door.”
Lucia looked back the way they had come. The parking lot was wide open, with nothing around it but cars and sky. “So Mateo's hello just kept going,” she said.

“How far away is that wall?” Lucia asked. Aunt Rosa pressed a button to turn her big sports watch into a stopwatch, then handed it to Lucia. “Mateo, shout one short word,” she said. “Lucia, press start when he shouts and stop when the echo comes back.”
Mateo planted his feet and shouted, “HEY!” Lucia pressed start with a beep and held her breath. When the wall said hey back, she pressed stop. The numbers on the watch said 1 second.
“Sound is fast,” said Aunt Rosa. “It goes about 340 meters in one second.” Lucia wrote 340 in her notebook.
She looked up. “So the wall is 340 meters away?” “Not so fast,” said Aunt Rosa. “Your hey had to get to the wall, and then it had to come all the way back.”
Lucia frowned at the wall. Then she drew a stick-figure Mateo, a big flat wall and two arrows, one going there and one coming back. She tapped her pencil on the 340 and started to divide.

Mateo had bigger plans. He cupped his hands and took his biggest breath yet. “MATEO IS THE GREATEST HIKER IN THE WHOLE WORLD!” He was only halfway through when the start of it came flying back. His voice and the echo tumbled over each other, like five kids talking at once.
Mateo scowled. “It talked over me. I need a bigger canyon.” “Or a shorter sentence,” said Lucia.
Aunt Rosa unfolded the trail map and tapped the dot at the very end, where it said ECHO POINT. “Four kilometers,” she said. “Your bigger canyon is waiting.” Mateo was already marching up the trail.

art.s: At the first bend of a red-striped desert canyon, an eight-year-old boy shouts with cupped hands toward a tall flat rock wall while his nine-year-old cousin holds a stopwatch and a notebook.

q.q: In the parking lot, Mateo's hello never came back. Why not?
c: There was no wall for it to bounce off.
He did not shout loud enough.
The cars soaked up all the sound.
The wind blew the sound away.
q.e: An echo needs something hard to bounce off. The parking lot was wide open, so the hello just kept going.

q.q: Draw Mateo shouting “PIZZA!” and the canyon answering. Write the words so we can see which one is louder.
look: Mateo's word in big capital letters
the canyon's word in smaller letters
q.e: Big capital letters mean a big shout. The echo came back smaller, so its letters are smaller too.

q.q: In 1 second, the hey went about 340 meters, to the wall and back. How far away was the wall?
q.e: 340 meters was the whole trip, there and back. Half of 340 is 170, so the wall was about 170 meters away.

eps.t: The Hill That Ate the Clap
p: Mateo dragged his sneakers through the sand, scritch, scratch, scritch, all the way up the trail. “We've been hiking for hours and hours,” he said. Lucia checked Aunt Rosa's watch. They had left the parking lot at 9:20, and now it was 10:05.
“Not hours,” Lucia said, “not even one.” Mateo shrugged. “It feels like hours, and feelings count.”

Aunt Rosa stopped at a short wooden post with 1 KM carved into it. The canyon was wide and open here. On the right side of the trail stood a smooth wall of pale rock. Right next to it, a hill of thick grass and scratchy bushes rose toward the sky. “Snack stop,” said Aunt Rosa, and she sat down on a flat stone.

Mateo faced the grassy hill and shouted his favorite word, “PIZZA!” The hill did not say pizza back, or anything else at all. Mateo tried again, even louder, until his face turned as red as his cap, but the hill stayed quiet.
“I just need to be louder,” Mateo said. Lucia shook her head and pointed at the hill with her pencil. “You were plenty loud. It's the grass.”
Mateo crossed his arms. “Grass can't eat sound.” Lucia crossed hers too. “Maybe it can.”
Aunt Rosa passed around a bag of cheese crackers and looked from one cousin to the other. “You two could argue all day, or you could test it,” she said.

Lucia made the rules, because Lucia always made the rules. Mateo had the loudest clap, so he would do the clapping. First he would stand 40 big steps from the rock wall and clap once. Then he would stand 40 big steps from the grassy hill and clap once, just as hard. Same clapper, same clap, same number of steps.

Mateo counted his steps out loud, taking giant strides like a giraffe, all the way to forty. He turned to face the pale rock and clapped. The echo came back so fast that it almost stuck to the clap. Clap-ap! Lucia made a mark in her notebook.

Next came the grassy hill. A small lizard on a rock watched them and did three quick push-ups. Mateo counted forty giant steps away from the hill, turned around and clapped just as hard. This time there was only one clap. He clapped again and again until his hands stung, but the grass swallowed every clap.

“It ate my clap,” Mateo said, glaring at the hill as if it had stolen his sandwich. Aunt Rosa brushed the crumbs off her knees. “Grass and bushes are soft and full of tiny gaps,” she said. “They soak up sound, like a sponge soaks up spilled milk. Hard rock sends it right back.”
Lucia drew a tiny table in her notebook with two rows. One said Rock wall: echo, and one said Grassy hill: no echo. Mateo read it upside down and let out a long sigh. “Fine, the grass wins,” he said.

He flopped face-first into a patch of grass beside the trail to show there were no hard feelings. The grass tickled his nose, and his nose began to twitch. Mateo rolled over toward the rock wall just in time. “Ah-ah-AH-CHOO!”
A moment later, the rock wall sneezed right back, only a little quieter. Lucia looked at the wall and said, “Bless you.”

art.s: On a canyon trail, a boy claps toward a hillside of thick grass and bushes while his cousin writes in a notebook and his mom sits on a flat stone with crackers; a smooth pale rock wall rises right beside the grassy hill.

q.q: They left the parking lot at 9:20. Lucia checked the watch at 10:05. How long had they been hiking?
c: 35 minutes
45 minutes
55 minutes
1 hour 45 minutes
q.e: From 9:20 to 10:00 is 40 minutes. Five more minutes makes 45. Not hours after all!

q.q: Why didn't Mateo's clap come back from the grassy hill?
q.a: The soft grass and bushes soaked up the sound, so it did not bounce back.
q.e: Soft, bumpy things soak up sound. Hard, smooth rock bounces it back.

q.q: The story says the rock wall “sneezed right back.” Draw the wall sneezing at Mateo. You choose its face.
look: the rock wall with a face
an AH-CHOO coming from the wall
q.e: A wall can't really sneeze. The story says it that way because the echo sounded just like Mateo's sneeze.

p: At the post marked 2 KM, Mateo flopped onto a rock like a dropped backpack. “My legs say we're almost there,” he said. “Ten more steps, tops.” Lucia unfolded the trail map across her knees.

The trail was a wiggly red line from the parking lot to Echo Point. Little marks cut it into four equal parts, one for each kilometer. Lucia put her finger on the second mark. “Your legs are wrong,” she said. “Two parts done, two to go.”

Mateo let his head drop back against the rock, but Aunt Rosa just pointed down the trail. There the walls leaned closer and closer until only a dark slit of path was left between them. “That's the Narrows,” she said. “Best part of the whole hike.”

Inside, the air was cool, like the air from an open fridge. The walls were so close that Mateo could touch both of them with his arms out. The rock felt smooth and a little damp under his fingers. Far above, the sky was a thin blue ribbon.

Somewhere a drop of water fell into a tiny puddle, plink, and even that small sound rang against the rock. Lucia stopped in the middle of the Narrows and clapped once. Brrrrrap! The clap buzzed and rattled like a stick dragged fast along a fence.

It lasted much longer than a clap should. Lucia stared at her hands as if they had done a magic trick. Mateo clapped too, again and again, faster and faster. Then he shouted, “It's a clap machine!” and the walls shouted it back in a hundred buzzy pieces.

Aunt Rosa covered her ears until he stopped. “Two flat walls, very close, facing each other,” she said. “Your clap hits one wall and bounces to the other. Then it bounces back again, over and over, like a Ping-Pong ball in a tiny box.” Mateo whipped his head from one wall to the other, as if he could see it go.

Lucia leaned on the cool wall and wrote in her notebook, “My clap went back and forth between the walls.” Mateo read it over her shoulder and wrinkled his nose. “Went is a boring word,” he said. “That clap didn't just go, it zipped!”
Lucia looked at the word for a long moment. The clap had moved so fast that nobody could count the bounces. She crossed out “went” and wrote “zipped” on top. Mateo gave her two thumbs up.

Next, Mateo tried out a long sentence, “MATEO IS THE KING OF THE CANYON!” The Narrows chewed it up and spat it out as one long buzz, like a bee stuck in a tin can. Lucia snorted, and the walls snorted back.
“Too long, and these walls are too close,” said Aunt Rosa. “Save your big words for Echo Point.” Mateo zipped his lips shut with two fingers, which made Lucia snort all over again.

At the far end, they squeezed out of the Narrows into bright, hot sunshine. Mateo turned around, leaned back into the cool shadow and clapped one last time. Brrrap! Then he waved goodbye to the clap machine.

art.s: Inside a narrow slot canyon with smooth, damp red walls, a girl claps while her cousin touches both walls with his arms stretched out, and a thin strip of blue sky shows far above.

q.q: The map showed 4 equal parts. At the 2 KM post, what fraction of the trail had they walked?
q.e: Two parts done out of four equal parts is 2/4. That's the same as half the trail!

q.q: Lucia changed “went” to “zipped.” Why is “zipped” a better word for her clap?
q.a: Because the clap moved super fast, and “zipped” sounds fast. “Went” is a boring word.
q.e: Strong verbs help us hear what happened. “Zipped” sounds just as fast as that clap.

q.q: Draw Lucia clapping in the Narrows. Use arrows to show where her clap went.
look: arrows bouncing back and forth between the walls
q.e: Zip, zip, zip! Your arrows show the clap bouncing like a Ping-Pong ball.

p: Past the 3 KM post, a rock ledge stuck out over the trail like the brim of a giant hat. A ranger sat in its cool blue shadow with a clipboard on her knees. Her name tag said RANGER KIM.

Mateo ran ahead into the shade and filled his lungs for his biggest HELLO yet. Then Lucia saw a little sign beside the ranger. It said QUIET PLEASE, BATS SLEEPING. She clapped her hand over Mateo's mouth just in time, and his hello came out as a muffled hmmph.

Ranger Kim put a finger to her lips and pointed up at a long crack in the ledge. Lucia squinted into the shadows. Deep inside, a row of brown, fuzzy shapes hung upside down, each one about as long as her thumb.

“They look like tiny folded umbrellas,” Lucia whispered. “They hunted all night, and now they sleep all day,” Ranger Kim whispered back. In the quiet, Mateo's stomach let out a long, loud growl, and one bat twitched an ear. Mateo froze like a statue until it went still again.

Then he leaned closer to Ranger Kim and whispered, “I have a bat at home, and it lives in my closet.” Ranger Kim raised her eyebrows. “What does it eat?” “Baseballs,” said Mateo, and Lucia had to press her sleeve over her mouth to keep the laugh in.

Ranger Kim held up a picture of a fat gray moth. “This is what real bats eat,” she whispered. “They catch them at night, when it's too dark to see much. So each bat makes tiny squeaks, too high for our ears to hear.”
She tapped the moth in the picture. “The squeaks bounce off the bug and come back to the bat.” Mateo's mouth fell open. “They use echoes, like us!” he whispered.
“Like you, only better,” said Ranger Kim. “A bat can find one moth in the dark, in midair, just by listening.”

She turned her clipboard around so they could see it. Every evening at sunset, she sat under the ledge with a little counter in her hand. Click, click, click went the counter, one click for each bat that flew out. Her table said Monday 40, Tuesday 60 and Wednesday 30.
“Why so few on Wednesday?” Lucia asked. Ranger Kim shrugged. “Some moved to a different crack. Bats don't tell me their plans.”
Lucia flipped to a clean page and drew three quick bars, one for each night. Mateo pointed at the shortest one. “That bar is taking a nap too,” he whispered.

Before they left, Lucia showed Ranger Kim her echo page. The top line said First Bend: 1 second. Ranger Kim tapped the line with her pen. “The wall at Echo Point is three times as far away as that one,” she said. “Say something short up there, and then wait.”

Mateo tiptoed out from under the ledge, one giant quiet step at a time. At the edge of the shade, he turned around. “Sleep tight, bats,” he whispered. Up in the crack, the row of fuzzy umbrellas did not move at all.

art.s: Under a shady rock ledge on a canyon trail, a park ranger with a clipboard points up at small brown bats sleeping upside down in a crack while two cousins whisper beside her.

q.q: Mateo said his bat at home eats baseballs. What kind of bat does Mateo really have?
q.a: A baseball bat, the kind you hit balls with.
q.e: Bat has two meanings: a flying animal and a stick for hitting balls. Mateo was making a joke!

q.q: How do the bats find moths in the dark?
c: They listen for echoes of their squeaks.
They sniff the air for moth smells.
They wait for moths to land on them.
They follow the light of the moon.
q.e: Squeak, bounce, listen! The echo tells a bat where the moth is.

q.q: Ranger Kim counted 40 bats on Monday, 60 on Tuesday and 30 on Wednesday. Draw a bar graph.
look: three bars, one for each night
Tuesday's bar is the tallest and Wednesday's is the shortest
numbers or labels so we can read it
q.e: Now anyone can see which night had the most bats, just by looking!

p: The last kilometer went up, up, up. The trail zigzagged back and forth across a steep slope, and Mateo counted every turn out loud. At turn number eleven, the ground went flat. They were standing on a wide shelf of rock beside a metal sign that said ECHO POINT.

In front of them, the canyon opened like a giant bowl. On the far side stood one huge, smooth wall, glowing orange in the sun. It looked close enough to touch. Then Lucia spotted the tiny trees at its feet, no bigger than broccoli, and she knew it was far.

Lucia opened her notebook to her echo page. At First Bend, the echo had taken 1 second. Ranger Kim had said this wall was three times as far away. “I bet it takes 3 seconds,” Lucia said, and she wrote her guess at the bottom of the page. “The sound goes three times as far there, and three times as far back.”

Aunt Rosa set her watch to zero and handed it to Lucia. Mateo had been planning his message for four whole kilometers. This time it was short, only three words. He whispered it once while Lucia timed him: 2 seconds. “It'll be done before the echo gets back,” she said.

Then he stepped up to the edge of the shelf and forgot everything. “MATEO WAS HERE AND LUCIA WAS HERE AND MOM WAS HERE AND—” The canyon started answering before he was done. His voice and the echo crashed into each other like bumper cars. Aunt Rosa laughed until she had to sit down on her backpack.

Mateo's ears went pink. “I added stuff,” he said. “Just the short one this time,” said Lucia. Mateo shook out his arms like a swimmer before a race and took a big breath. Lucia put her thumb on the start button.

“MATEO WAS HERE!” Lucia pressed start on the very first word, and then Mateo shut his mouth tight. One second passed, then two. The canyon went so quiet that Lucia could hear a bird singing somewhere far below.

At three, the words rolled back across the canyon, with nothing talking over them this time. “Mateo was here!” Lucia pressed stop, and Mateo grabbed her arm with both hands. “It said all of it,” he whispered. “It said my whole message!”

The watch said 3 seconds. Lucia circled her guess. On the next line of her table she wrote Echo Point: 3 seconds, and under that, 3 × 340 = 1,020 meters. “But that's there and back,” she said, and she worked out one more step.

Then it was Lucia's turn, and she did not need anything long. She cupped her hands and shouted her favorite word from the whole day, “ZIPPED!” Three seconds later, the far wall zipped it right back to her.

Beside the sign stood a metal box with a notebook inside for hikers. Mateo wrote in giant letters: MATEO WAS HERE. THE WALL SAID SO. Lucia wrote her name underneath, and next to it, how far away the wall was. Aunt Rosa added a tiny drawing of a pizza.
Then all three of them faced the orange wall and shouted together, “PIZZA!” The canyon waited three whole seconds, and then it agreed.

art.s: On a wide rock shelf at Echo Point, a boy shouts across a huge canyon toward a glowing orange wall while his cousin holds a stopwatch and his mom laughs, sitting on her backpack.

q.q: What is this part of the story mostly about?
c: Mateo finally hears his whole message come back.
Aunt Rosa laughs and sits on her backpack.
Lucia writes her name in the hikers' notebook.
A bird sings somewhere far below the rock.
q.e: All four things happened. The big idea is Mateo's whole message coming back at last.

q.q: Lucia wrote 3 × 340 = 1,020 meters. That was there and back. How far away was the wall?
q.e: The trip to the wall is half of the whole trip. Half of 1,020 is 510 meters.

q.q: Draw the First Bend wall and the Echo Point wall. Use arrows to show why one echo took longer.
look: the Echo Point wall much farther away
longer arrows to the far wall and back
1 second and 3 seconds written by the walls
q.e: Farther wall, longer trip, longer wait. Your drawing explains it!

fin.q: No echo came back in the parking lot or from the grassy hill. What was missing in both places?
fin.a: A hard, smooth rock wall for the sound to bounce off.
fin.e: Echoes need something hard to bounce off. Open air and soft grass don't send sound back.

fin.q: How were Lucia and Mateo different on the hike?
c: Lucia timed and wrote things down. Mateo shouted first.
Lucia shouted the loudest. Mateo kept the notebook.
Lucia wanted to go home. Mateo wanted to stay longer.
Lucia ran ahead. Mateo stayed close to his mom.
fin.e: Lucia measured and Mateo shouted. Together they found every echo on the trail!
